# Mahāvedalla Sutta (MN 43 (PTS MN i 292))

**ID:** MN 43 (PTS MN i 292)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Mahāvedalla Sutta
**PTS:** MN i 292
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0201m.mul4.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahāvedalla Sutta* (MN 43) is an analytical catechism set in Sāvatthī, taking the form of a dialogue between the Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita [Klaus and Hartmann 2007]. Mahākoṭṭhita questions Sāriputta concerning abstruse doctrinal topics, including the mutual inseparability of wisdom (*paññā*), consciousness (*viññāṇa*), feeling (*vedanā*), and perception (*saññā*), which are described as conjoined (*saṃsaṭṭha*) rather than separate mental phenomena [Hung 2010; Nakamura 1980]. The discourse also outlines the five factors supporting right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*) that lead to deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom [Melnikova 2014], the three elements sustaining the living physical body—vitality (*āyu*), heat (*usmā*), and consciousness (*viññāṇa*) [Hung 2010; Hayashi 2013], the limbs of the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) [Deleanu 2006], and various classifications of mind-deliverance (*cetovimutti*), such as the immeasurable, nothingness, emptiness, and signless liberations [Peoples 2013; Yinshun].

The commentary (*Papañcasūdanī*) describes the dialogue as an inquiry to compare views (*diṭṭhasaṃsandanāpucchā*) and highlights Mahākoṭṭhita's renown for analytical knowledge (*paṭisambhidā*) [Klaus and Hartmann 2007]. Modern scholars note that the text's systematic categorization and definitions of disparate concepts reflect a proto-Abhidharmic stratum of the Suttapiṭaka, representing a transitional development toward scholastic systematization [Analayo 2014; Deleanu 2006]. While the Pali canon pairs this sutta with the *Cūḷavedalla Sutta* under the genre term *vedalla*, northern parallels are instead named after the interlocutors as the *Mahākauṣṭhila-sūtra* [Nyanatusita 2013].

 Comparative studies demonstrate that MĀ 211 places the setting at Rājagaha rather than Sāvatthī, inverts the roles of interrogator and respondent, omits the first absorption limb analysis found in the Pali text, and shares content that the Pali tradition locates in the *Cūḷavedalla Sutta* [Deleanu 2006; Klaus and Hartmann 2007; Yinshun].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Resembling parallels: MA 211 大拘絺羅; AN 4.175 Upavāṇasutta; SA 251 拘絺羅; Up 3.064; Up 9.008

**Sources**

- [Nyanatusita 2013] Bhikkhu Nyanatusita (ed.), Bodhisattva Ideal: Essays on the Emergence of Mahāyāna (2013) — Discussion of the title Vedalla versus Sanskrit titles like Mahākauṣṭhila-sūtra.
- [Peoples 2013] Dion Peoples, Buddhist Critical Thinking Skills (2013) — Summary of doctrinal themes including meditations, factors of mind, and deliverance.
- [Deleanu 2006] Florin Deleanu, The Chapter on the Mundane Path (Laukikamārga) in the Śrāvakabhūmi, Vol. 2 (2006) — Identification of Chinese parallels (T 211, T 251), proto-Abhidharmic style, and absorption factors.
- [Nakamura 1980] Hajime Nakamura, Indian Buddhism: A Survey with Bibliographical Notes (1980) — Citation of modern scholarship on paññā and viññāṇa in MN 43.
- [Klaus and Hartmann 2007] Konrad Klaus and Jens-Uwe Hartmann (eds.), Indica et Tibetica: Festschrift für Michael Hahn (2007) — Papañcasūdanī commentary citation and comparison of setting and interlocutors with MĀ 211.
- [Yinshun] Yinshun, Investigations into Śūnyatā — Comparison of types of mind-release and samādhis between MN 43, SN, and MĀ 211.
- [Hung 2010] Ya-Chun Hung (Bhikkhuni Syinchen), Issues in Samatha and Vipaśyanā: A Comparative Study of Buddhist Meditation (2010) — Quotes on conjoined mental states (paññā/viññāṇa, feeling/perception/consciousness) and vitality/heat/consciousness.
- [Melnikova 2014] Nora Melnikova, Modern School of Vipassanā – A Buddhist Tradition (2014) — Citation of MN i 292 regarding the five factors supporting right view.
- [Hayashi 2013] Itsuki Hayashi, Rehabilitating Momentariness: A Critical Revision of the Buddhist Doctrine of Momentariness (2013) — Discussion of vitality, heat, and consciousness, citing Thanissaro Bhikkhu's translation.
